A “small convocation” is a named communal address, often held in the evening or for a special occasion, whose procedure and content are less fixed than an ordinary hall address. The Baizhang rules say it has no fixed location, may use the sleeping hall or teaching hall according to attendance, is announced by a placard, omits the release-from-consultation bell, gathers the community after the evening bell, and lets the resident master mount the seat. The same rules list occasions including installation, visiting officials or donors, special requests, instruction for the dead, and seasonal observances. Records then mark small convocations for year-end, opening or closing a retreat, memorial instruction, ordination, and ordinary evening teaching. A playful interview answers “what is a small convocation?” with “eating gruel,” contrasting a great convocation with eating rice. These uses identify an event format, not a diminutive teaching.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 7,411 hits in 357 files and 353 works. Eight curated witnesses from seven works meet the floor and include both procedural definition and performed events.

Senses.Explanation: Dahui directly defines dull sinking by contrast: forgetting and falling into a dark cave is called dull sinking, while deliberate mental succession is called agitation. Literally, dim or dull sinking . Dahui supplies the corpus's clearest direct description: forgetting or blanking out falls into the ghost cave beneath Black Mountain, and the teachings call this dull sinking; he contrasts it with deliberate attention, whose thought-consciousness flies about and is called agitation. Other records label dull sinking “not good” beside “binding thought strays from the real” and pair it repeatedly with agitation as the two named conditions found in the Chan hall. The Chan record also bends the inherited fault-category against simple rejection: Gaofeng says the four graphs “dull sinking and agitation” are themselves buddha-nature, Daodu calls the pair one's place for establishing life, and Dahui tells Lü Juren that whether dull-sunk or agitated, it is still only Lü Juren. The deviation lies in this combination of exact diagnosis, fixed pairing, and masters' refusal to locate the named condition outside the person who reports it.

To leak out or show through. Chan records most often use the expression as a retrospective appraisal after someone has spoken or acted: 'it leaked out,' 'quite a lot leaked out,' 'the whole body leaked out,' or 'one could not avoid leaking once.' Foyan applies the same verdict in succession to Deshan's statement that his house has no phrases and no single thing to give people, Xuefeng's statement that he went empty-handed and returned empty-handed, and Muzhou's calling an unnamed monk a board-carrying fellow. The Blue Cliff Record says that much had leaked out when Bodhidharma pressed Emperor Wu at the outset. A later direct question, 'What is the place of leaking out?' receives a list of recorded expressions and objects: Yunmen's flatbread, Zhaozhou's tea, Xuefeng's wooden ball, and Zihu's dog. The records do not identify a single substance that leaks, and this entry adds none.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 488 matches in 172 files. 'It leaked out' occurs sixty times in thirty-seven files; 'quite a lot leaked out' occurs eighty-one times in fifty-four; 'the whole body leaked out' occurs twice in two; and 'could not avoid leaking out' occurs twice in two. One passage in one file directly asks where leaking out is. The two nominal-looking matches ending in 'one who leaks' are parts of late verse lines about a portrait or a festival wrapper and do not supply a separate definition.

SearchAliases: a golden-scaled fish through the net
Senses.Explanation: A golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net figures an exceptional adept no longer caught by ordinary devices. The phrase is anchored in Sansheng’s public question to Xuefeng: “What does the golden-scaled fish through the net feed on?” (透網金鱗未審以何為食); Xuefeng replies that he will tell him after he comes out of the net. Yuanwu’s prose supplies the corpus’s direct definition: “only with an eye at the crown is one called a golden-scaled fish through the net” (頂門有眼方謂之透網金鱗). The image then becomes an appraisal of monks: Baowen Hongyin hails a patch-robed monastic as “excellent—a patch-robed monk, a golden-scaled fish through the net” (俊哉衲子，透網金鱗), while later interviews ask why such a fish is still held up by water.

Senses.Explanation: To pass the barrier is to get through a tested obstruction: the records contrast those already through with those still stopped, and extend the phrase to a barrier-passing eye and phrase. Huanglong Huinan distinguishes the two conditions: 'one already past the barrier swings his arms and goes straight on' (已過關者掉臂徑去), whereas 'this is one who has not passed the barrier' (此未透關者也). Zhongfeng Mingben records a corrective contrast: people thread all old and new public cases onto one string and call it 'passing the barrier' (謂之透關), while 'the tight barrier of life and death beneath their heels has not actually been passed' (脚跟下一座生死牢關，政好不曾透得). The phrase also builds 'an eye that passes the barrier' (透關眼). Yuanwu Keqin asks whether anyone present has such an eye. Chijue Daochong says, 'Passing the barrier requires a barrier-passing eye; obtaining treasure requires one who can distinguish treasure' (透關須具透關眼，得寶須還別寶人). Poshan Haiming answers the question 'What is a phrase that passes the barrier?' (如何是透關句), and Dabian Xianquan contrasts 'one already through the barrier' (已透關者) with 'one not through the barrier' (未透關者). These are recorded descriptions, corrections, and compounds; this entry adds no unrecorded destination beyond the barrier.
